claims.text: A gradient nanostructure can simultaneously increase metal strength while maintaining or enhancing ductility.
The proposed gradient has grain size decreasing from the core toward the surface.
Severe plastic deformation can introduce the proposed gradient nanostructure.
Surface mechanical grinding treatment or surface mechanical attrition can form a gradient-nanostructured surface layer.
Appropriate heat treatment following surface deformation contributes to formation of the proposed gradient structure.
Moderate processing temperatures and suitable strain rates can produce a graded microstructural transition without excessive bulk recrystallization.
The structural mediator is a depth-dependent transition from nanocrystalline or ultrafine surface grains to a coarser-grained interior.
Ultrafine surface grains impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion in the ultrafine-grained surface increases strength.
Coarser grains in the interior permit greater plastic deformation.
Plastic deformation accommodated by the coarser-grained interior maintains ductility.
The gradient-structured metal is predicted to have higher yield strength than its conventional counterpart.
The yield-strength increase could be approximately 20–30% relative to the conventional counterpart.
The gradient-structured metal is predicted to retain or increase ductility while its strength increases.
Homogeneously fine-grained or coarse-grained metals generally exhibit an inverse relationship between strength and ductility.
Very high strain rates may diminish the beneficial effect of the gradient nanostructure.
Elevated temperatures may diminish the beneficial effect by causing dynamic recrystallization or coarsening of the gradient nanostructure.
The magnitudes of the strength and ductility improvements depend on processing-parameter optimization.
